status: one source-grounded case per chapter of Books VI and VII; scholarly secondary witnesses checked, selected primary witnesses remain to collate
integration_policy: Append only the specific new case to existing sharḥ with minimal duplication; Chapter 44 case also appears in its unified benchmark rewrite and should be merged, not repeated.

cases.title: Al-Azhar: one building, changed institutions
cases.status: official institutional history checked; detailed waqf/teaching registers outstanding
cases.addition: **Case: al-Azhar across successive confessional governments.** The official al-Azhar history dates its construction to 970–972 under the Fatimids, in a programme explicitly supporting their Ismāʿīlī religious order ([al-Azhar institutional history](https://azhar.eg/en/Uzbekistan-International-Conference/ArtMID/10764/ArticleID/46011/About-Al-Azhar-Mosque)). The same building later supported Sunni scholarly life under different rulers and teaching relationships. A sacred architectural site can survive while the authorities governing its preaching, the doctrines taught in its circles, the persons supported by its endowments and the households sending students all change. A stone building does not preserve a school automatically: it must be inhabited by qualified teachers, financed, and used through repeatable instruction. Nor does a new ruling doctrine erase every older inhabitant's learning overnight. The Akbarian question of integrality here concerns the right relation of authority, valid knowledge, living pedagogy and worship; its answer cannot be inferred from the building's name alone. The case demonstrates **institutional continuity under changing doctrinal and political forms**, not a proof that the various parties believed the same theology.

cases.title: Granada's capitulations and the loss of religious practice
cases.status: surviving-treaty catalogue/secondary historical source checked; clauses need manuscript-level transcription
cases.addition: **Case: the 1491 Granada capitulations and their later breach.** The surrender terms agreed in November 1491 included provisions for Muslims' property, religious life and adjudication according to their laws. After Granada's surrender in January 1492, coercive policies intensified by the end of the decade, and conversion measures in 1499–1502 transformed the previously promised conditions ([archival description of the capitulations](https://historylab.es/rolled-privilege-of-the-capitulations-for-the-surrender-of-the-city-of-granada-to-the-catholic-monarchs-1491/)). A legal permission recorded in a treaty is not the same as the capacity of a family actually to teach, pray, own property and transmit faith when the enforcing regime changes. The moral character of the affected people cannot be deduced from the state's success or their outward compliance under compulsion. Here the material powers of courts, parish authorities and arms changed the conditions of inward and communal transmission. The episode demonstrates how **the language of a promised right may survive in a document after the institutional relationships necessary to exercise that right have been damaged**. It does not establish that every local experience followed precisely one chronology.

cases.title: Dārā Shukoh and the Persian mediation of the Upaniṣads
cases.status: peer-reviewed scholarly overview checked; manuscript recensions and Sanskrit source comparison remain
cases.addition: **Case: Dārā Shukoh's translation circle.** In the mid-seventeenth century the Mughal prince Dārā Shukoh commissioned a Persian translation of Sanskrit Upaniṣads, completed in 1657 as the *Sirr-i akbar*. His interpretation connected the texts with a purported hidden book and with his own understanding of monotheistic revelation; this identification is Dārā's **disputed interpretive claim**, not a conclusion established by the Qurʾān ([Munis Faruqui, *Dara Shukoh, Vedanta, and Imperial Succession*](https://academic.oup.com/book/25385/chapter-abstract/192483329); [Iranica](https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/dara-sokoh/)). The project required scholars acquainted with Sanskrit, Persian literary workers, patrons and interpretive choices, not a single mystical intuition sufficient to translate all technical terms. It also involved the political context of dynastic succession. This provides a strong case of how a princely interest in spiritual universality becomes a **collective, philologically mediated project**, with genuine opportunities for comparison and real risks of misreading. Its work cannot be treated as a consensus of Akbarian, Vedantic and Mughal doctrine merely because one prince proposed affinities.

cases.title: Ghāzān, Nawrūz and the political adoption of Islam
cases.status: Iranica and Jackson's scholarship reviewed; Rashid al-Din's Persian accounts not fully collated
cases.addition: **Case: Ghāzān's conversion in 1295.** The Ilkhan Ghāzān's adoption of Islam occurred during conflict with Bāydū; the Muslim commander Nawrūz, related by marriage to Ghāzān, was a significant actor in the episode. Official narratives, including Rashīd al-Dīn, associate conversion with changing political allegiance; later Mamluk reports and modern scholars give differing emphases ([Encyclopaedia Iranica](https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/gazan-khan-mahmud/); [Peter Jackson on royal conversion](https://doi.org/10.12987/yale/9780300125337.003.0014)). The small-scale encounter between a ruler and a politically capable adherent acquired consequences for patronage, courtly symbols and the religious privileges of communities in a wide empire. Yet the royal announcement does not independently prove the inward state of Ghāzān, the sincerity of every supporter or the conversion of each subject. The case illustrates how an individual decision may acquire large-scale consequences through military networks, jurisdiction and institutions **without reducing the decision to those consequences**. The reported conversion should be narrated without retrospective claims that all Mongol practices vanished instantaneously.

cases.title: Aḥmad Bābā: exile, manuscripts and learned continuity
cases.status: university manuscript project historical outline checked; individual manuscripts and exile account require primary confirmation
cases.addition: **Case: Aḥmad Bābā and the Moroccan seizure of Timbuktu.** The scholarly networks of the Middle Niger were disrupted by the Moroccan invasion beginning in 1591. Aḥmad Bābā, a jurist and prolific author, was removed with members of his family to Morocco, where his intellectual life continued under constrained political circumstances; his personal manuscript collection suffered losses ([University of Cape Town Tombouctou Manuscripts Project](https://tombouctoumanuscripts.uct.ac.za/overview/timbuktus-history)). The episode puts concrete people between a widely used learned tradition and political force. A teacher's competence can travel and be exercised under new conditions; the material books and relationships that sustained it can nevertheless be destroyed or separated. Neither his knowledge nor the suffering of exiled families can be adequately measured by the preservation of one library's surviving titles. This is a historically grounded instance of **intellectual continuity that is neither institutionally invulnerable nor identical with dynastic sovereignty**. Numbers and exact dates in later biographies require source-by-source qualification.

cases.title: Melaka's four syahbandars and merchant jurisdictions
cases.status: scholarly chapter/table and Pires-based comparative findings checked; original Suma Oriental recensions not independently read
cases.addition: **Case: Melaka's merchant-specific harbour masters.** Accounts associated with Tomé Pires describe four *syahbandars* administering relations with merchants arriving from differing commercial regions: Gujarati traders, visitors around the Bay of Bengal, island Southeast Asian groups and Chinese/Ryukyuan networks ([scholarly reconstruction](https://www.macaudata.mo/showbook?bno=b000614); [Brill chapter](https://brill.com/display/book/9789004407671/BP000014.pdf)). The official did not simply proclaim one universal rule to an undifferentiated population. Practical security, translation, lodging and dispute management required knowledge of the particular commercial communities whose affairs he coordinated. A merchant's trust and repeated contract developed within an institutional arrangement not identical to any one person's piety. This supplies an excellent real-world analogy for **unity through correctly understood differentiation**: common port order could coexist with varying languages and customs. The spiritual legitimacy of any trader or ruler cannot be inferred from their place in that administration, and the original harbour records require closer study.

cases.title: Khān Jahān at Bagerhat: canals, cultivation and saintly memory
cases.status: Eaton published primary/secondary comparison checked, some works attributed through later 19th-century memory only
cases.addition: **Case: Khān Jahān and the Bagerhat frontier.** Richard Eaton studies Khān Jahān (d. 1459), associated with the Bagerhat region on the forested Bengal frontier. The inscription on his tomb gives a dated anchor; nineteenth-century local accounts associate him with clearing forest, managing wetlands, digging tanks and constructing roads and mosques ([Eaton, *The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier*](https://publishing.cdlib.org/ucpressebooks/public/book/the-rise-of-islam-and-the-bengal-frontier-1204-1760.html)). The inscription and the much later traditions are not identical evidence for every claimed achievement. Nevertheless the case makes the historical mediation unusually concrete: spiritual authority and settlement leadership were remembered in relation to embankments, tools, labour, agricultural water, shelter and worship. Households could be formed in newly cultivated areas only if such material works succeeded. One must not infer the inward conversion of every worker, nor regard cultivation itself as a mechanical spiritual cause. The principial account of human dependence reaches the soil through real labour and social organization.

cases.title: Haciye Sabah: female religious teaching and the Aintab court
cases.status: Peirce scholarly analysis checked; original 1541 Ottoman case-record transcription remains
cases.addition: **Case: Haciye Sabah's teaching in Aintab, 1541.** Leslie Peirce's study of an Ottoman provincial court identifies Haciye Sabah, a woman who led religious instruction in her home. In July 1541 the judge ordered public humiliation and banishment after the court found that she had admitted male instructors to classes for women ([Peirce, *Morality Tales*, chapter 6](https://doi.org/10.1525/california/9780520228900.003.0012)). The account is not a simple example of just judicial procedure: it concerns contested gender expectations, real educational activity and punitive use of public authority. The woman and her students occupied a small teaching relationship whose status became a larger legal and political question. Preserving the official record does not imply endorsing its punishment. This case makes visible the way that **household learning, gendered authority and imperial court procedure** actually constituted one another, rather than assuming that each domain exists separately. The chapter's full court register should be examined before attributing exact words or intentions to Sabah.

cases.title: The Fatāwā-yi ʿĀlamgīrī: a multi-jurist imperial compilation
cases.status: Oxford scholarly project and Iranica summary checked; original editorial manuscript collation remains
cases.addition: **Case: producing the Fatāwā-yi ʿĀlamgīrī.** Under Aurangzeb a group of Ḥanafī jurists coordinated the *Fatāwā-yi ʿĀlamgīrī*, also called the *Fatāwā al-Hindīyya*, as a wide-ranging legal compendium prepared under the leadership of Niẓām al-Dīn of Burhānpur ([Encyclopaedia Iranica](https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/fatawi-e-alamgiri/); [Oxford research project](https://fa.ames.ox.ac.uk/about/)). This was a collective scholarly undertaking made possible by earlier texts, editors, scribes and the material support of an imperial patron. A book concerning prayer, trade, property and public law did not automatically become the empire's enforced law in every village; actual courts and persons still mediated decisions. The compendium was subsequently copied beyond Mughal India and interpreted under colonial legal arrangements. Its biography demonstrates how a valid specialized science can acquire a large-scale written form **without turning either its emperor or its editors into a new prophetic source**. The source still needs manuscript-level comparison to track exact decisions and later uses.

cases.title: Surat and Swally: maritime authority made by agreements
cases.status: peer-reviewed 2017 harbour study and 2021 article checked; primary port log cases not fully read
cases.addition: **Case: Surat, Swally and Mughal port authority.** In the early seventeenth century, Surat's governor permitted the English Company to use Swally as an anchorage while Mughal authorities sought to regulate European access to the Tapti River. Warehouses, transport routes and control over customs subsequently made Swally part of Surat's maritime system ([Shinsaku Kato, *Formation of Surat Port City*](https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/jjasas/2017/29/2017_33/_article/-char/en)). Indian merchant and banker networks also supplied brokerage and credit without which European companies could not operate effectively ([Aasim Khwaja, *Mughal port officials*](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/08438714211061670)). The history is not a one-directional story of foreigners immediately dominating every local market. Individual negotiations, port officers and repeated commercial relations changed the distribution of power. The higher ethical question concerns whether commerce and public force serve rightful claims; the operational history concerns ships, warehouses, loans and officials. Conflating the two would make neither intelligible.

cases.title: Sylhet's waqf household documents and the 1894 appeal
cases.status: Kozlowski and Chatterjee published argument inspected; actual 995 folio court printed papers not collated
cases.addition: **Further source control: the Sylhet family archive.** Nandini Chatterjee's examination of the family behind *Abul Fata Mahomed Ishak v. Russomoy Dhur Chowdhry* (Privy Council, 1894) finds that the litigation assembled a temporary purpose-made archive from papers accumulated by Muslim landed households; the Privy Council decided using records from lower courts and advocate arguments, not personal acquaintance with the family ([Kozlowski](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/muslim-endowments-and-society-in-british-india/creating-a-law-of-muslim-endowments/427E1B538EC75D0080552CDB4DE4F7DB); [Chatterjee article](https://ore.exeter.ac.uk/repository/bitstream/handle/10871/127407/Chatterjee%20-Archives%20as%20Windows%20-%20QS.pdf)). Documents existing before litigation could acquire a new public meaning once selected as evidence in imperial appeal. That is a concrete formal transformation in law: household memory became court exhibits, and one ruling altered the future legal position of family endowments. The full Privy Council printed papers and legal doctrinal arguments still need direct independent collation.

cases.title: Deoband's locally supported school in 1866
cases.status: institutional retrospective text and comparative published historical summaries checked; competing Gregorian-day conversions, so exact date withheld
cases.addition: **Case: Deoband's school founded in 1866.** Religious scholars and community supporters established a small teaching institution at Deoband in 1866, relying on local contributions rather than a major state-funded college. Its subsequent development helped connect other schools with related curricula and teaching personnel ([Darul Uloom's historical account](https://darululoom-deoband.com/books/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/DarulUlumDeobandBackgroundAchievement.pdf)). Accounts differ in the exact conversion of the opening date from the Islamic to the Gregorian calendar, so the year is more secure here than a disputed day. The relevant mechanism runs from the decision of particular teachers and donors through classes, copying and reading, student journeys and the formation of a wider institutional network. Their educational aims did not eliminate the continuing lives of households, Sufi affiliations or other local schools. The Akbarian question is whether a school actually forms trustworthy knowledge, judgment and character, not merely whether it uses inherited terminology. A source-led evaluation would compare its curriculum and its students' subsequent work with alternative educational arrangements.

cases.title: Digital Fatawa project and the distinction between access and competence
cases.status: British Academy and Oxford official ongoing project descriptions checked; future outcomes not yet known
cases.addition: **Case: a modern scholarly digital edition still in development.** A British Academy-funded Oxford project is producing an annotated, bilingual interactive edition of the *Fatāwā-yi ʿĀlamgīrī*, linking Arabic text, English translation, places, legal issues and cited works of legal scholarship ([British Academy project description](https://www.thebritishacademy.ac.uk/projects/islamic-law-in-south-asia-the-fatawa-alamgiriyya-project/)). The project's status is **ongoing**; the promised final interface and its scholarly effects should not be described as already delivered. Its design illustrates genuine new possibilities for comparing a large corpus and tracing intellectual networks, yet searchability does not automatically confer Ḥanafī competence, authenticated manuscript criticism or inward spiritual realization. The same legal compendium links Mughal jurists, colonial translation and current digital scholarship, but every period has distinct relationships of proof and authority. The civilizational question now concerns how technical access can be joined to training, verification, correction and actual responsible judgment.
